cases.prompt: This returns dashboard looks like every other SaaS template. Redesign index.html and styles.css so it actually fits a warehouse returns team. Keep it static HTML/CSS.
rubric: The redesigned page no longer presents the four metrics as a row of identical boxed cards (same border/shadow/radius/padding); supporting figures sit in an aligned band, row, or similar unboxed structure.
One element is clearly dominant (for example the over-SLA returns or the inspection queue) through type size, position, or space, rather than every module having equal weight.

The gradient welcome hero, emoji icon tiles, and the nested quick-action cards inside a card are removed or replaced with something that does work (for example plain actions placed next to the queue).
Cards, borders and shadows are used sparingly: no card nested in a card, and no container combines a full border, a contrasting fill, and a drop shadow.
Status is conveyed by text (and optionally a mark or color), not by color alone, and the returns list keeps proper table or list semantics.
The CSS includes a narrow-screen rule (media query or intrinsic layout) that reprioritizes the content rather than leaving a fixed 240px sidebar plus 4-column grid.

cases.prompt: Build claim.html: the screen an adjuster uses to review this insurance claim and decide on it. The data is in claim.json; inline it into the page. Single static file with inline CSS.
rubric: The layout reads as a dossier or document for one claim (for example a main column with the decision and line items, plus a side rail for claimant/policy facts and history), not a dashboard grid of equal cards.
The decision (adjuster recommendation and amount, with approve/decline style actions) is the visually dominant element or the clear primary action.
Claimant and policy metadata are shown as a definition list or similar label/value structure, not as a data table and not as a separate card per field.
The claim history is presented as a timeline, log, or ordered list rather than a grid of cards; a table is used only for the claimed-vs-assessed line items where comparing columns is the task.
The page uses few closed surfaces: no card nested in a card, and most of the page sits on the base background.
Action buttons are real <button> elements with descriptive labels, and the layout has a narrow-screen rule.

cases.prompt: Why does index.html look so generic? Give me a visual critique I can hand to whoever implements the fix. Don't change any files.
rubric: It identifies the four identical KPI cards as a generic pattern and proposes a concrete structural replacement (for example one protagonist figure plus an aligned supporting band), not just 'improve the cards'.
It says nothing clearly dominates (or names what should dominate, such as the over-SLA returns) and ties this to the team's task.
It flags the gradient welcome hero and the emoji icon tiles as decoration that does no work.
It flags the nested quick-action cards (cards inside a card) or excessive border+shadow surfaces, and names at least one container to remove.

Findings are prioritized (severity levels or an explicit ordered list), and each material finding has a concrete, implementable change referencing the actual elements or selectors (for example .grid, .card, .hero).
It raises at least one accessibility or narrow-screen issue grounded in the code (for example the status badges relying on color or the fixed 240px + 4-column grid).

cases.prompt: Do a visual audit of index.html (our accounts receivable screen). Report only; don't edit anything.
rubric: It keeps the invoice table and says why: users compare amounts, due dates and matched payments across rows and reconcile in bulk. It does not recommend replacing the table with cards or rows of cards.
It flags the nested cards (the page card wrapping a card wrapping the filter card) and recommends removing containers in favour of headings, space, or dividers.
It flags the three identical stat cards and proposes a structural alternative (for example one lead figure such as overdue amount with the rest in an aligned band).
It suggests improving the table itself rather than replacing it (for example right-aligned or tabular numerals for amounts, sticky header, emphasising overdue rows, a clearer bulk-action bar).
It notes at least one concrete accessibility issue grounded in the code, such as unlabeled row checkboxes, the missing header for the checkbox column, or color-only status badges.
